In August and September 1941, weeks after Germany invaded the Soviet Union, Stalin's government deported the whole Volga German people, about 400,000 people, to Kazakhstan and Siberia. A decree of 28 August accused them, without evidence, of hiding spies and saboteurs, and abolished their autonomous republic on the Volga.

The Volga Germans descended from farmers invited by Catherine the Great in the 1760s, who had kept their language and their Lutheran or Catholic faith for 180 years. They were given a day or two to pack, loaded onto cattle trains and scattered among collective farms and villages on the steppe. Germans from other parts of the Soviet Union followed, close to a million in all. Most men, and many women, were then drafted into the "labour army", working in camps where many died.

They stayed under special settlement rules until 1955 and were never allowed back to the Volga. Kazakhstan gained a large German minority. From the late 1980s, and above all after the Soviet collapse, most of them emigrated to Germany. The same method was used against the Chechens and Ingush in 1944.
